title: CDC Under Fire: Measles Deaths, Missing Data, and a Crisis of Trust
summary:
The United States is in the middle of its worst measles resurgence in decades. Vaccination rates are falling. Flu, COVID-19, and RSV are surging again. And now, many public health experts are asking a troubling question: can we trust the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention?

The controversy began when Pennsylvania state officials reported two deaths from measles. Normally, the state determines the cause of death, and the CDC shares that information to alert doctors and the public. But this time, Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. publicly questioned whether measles caused the deaths. The CDC then removed them from its website.

"Red flag. Red alert," says Dr. Demetre Daskalakis, who resigned last year as director of the CDC's National Center for Immunization and Respiratory Diseases. He left to protest what he called political interference. "When they raise doubt on the adjudication that a state may have made around a death, that is highly problematic," he says. "This is dangerous."

Dr. Anne Zink, a senior fellow at the Yale School of Public Health and former Alaska chief medical officer, agrees. "What we have been seeing, that got amplified even more with these measles cases, is a breakdown in the coordination and trust between states and the federal government," she says. "These partnerships are critical and essential to making us healthy and well."

Experts also worry about the CDC's new director, Dr. Erica Schwartz, who took over after a tumultuous year. Many hoped she would restore the agency's morale and credibility by pushing back against political pressure. But some say the handling of the Pennsylvania cases is a bad sign.

"We are seeing a pretty compromised CDC and a director who is at best facilitating non-scientific behavior and at worst colluding with non-scientific behavior," says Daskalakis.

Dr. Debra Houry, who resigned as CDC chief medical officer at the same time, wants Schwartz to focus on the outbreak. "I haven't heard from her talking about the importance of getting kindergarteners vaccinated when we're seeing declining rates," Houry says. "It's back to school time. We need her to step up publicly."

Neither the CDC nor HHS responded to NPR's requests for comment. For now, the question remains: if the public can't trust federal health data, who can they rely on?
why_it_matters: Outbreak control depends on public trust in a single shared set of facts: if states and the federal government stop trusting each other's data, vaccination campaigns and disease warnings get slower and weaker, and the people most at risk are children. This story is really about who gets to decide what counts as scientific truth — a question teenagers will keep meeting as citizens.

background_read: Measles is one of the most contagious viruses known: it can linger in the air of a room for up to two hours after a sick person leaves, and one infected person can sicken many unvaccinated people nearby. The MMR vaccine (two doses of the combined measles-mumps-rubella shot) is about 97% effective, which is why high vaccination rates are the main defense.

The United States declared measles 'eliminated' in 2000, meaning the virus no longer spread continuously inside the country. That status has been threatened repeatedly since; in 2019 the country recorded more than 1,200 cases, its highest count in decades, mostly in close-knit unvaccinated communities.

The CDC (the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, the federal agency that tracks disease and recommends vaccines) sits inside HHS (the Department of Health and Human Services, the cabinet department that oversees U.S. health agencies). Robert F. Kennedy Jr. (the HHS Secretary, who has for years questioned vaccine safety claims) leads that department and has been sharply criticized by public-health groups.

Normally, states investigate deaths and the CDC compiles and publishes the findings so doctors nationwide work from one consistent picture. The experts quoted in the article argue that when federal officials publicly doubt a state's finding, they damage the state-federal partnerships that make outbreak responses work.

perspectives.description: Some observers hope Dr. Erica Schwartz can steady an agency shaken by resignations and political fights, rebuilding morale and giving doctors a clear national voice. From this angle, a fresh director is a chance to restore routine functions like vaccine guidance and plain communication with states.

perspectives.perspective: Former CDC officials and public-health experts (critical)
perspectives.description: Daskalakis and Houry argue the opposite: that questioning a state's death findings and pulling them from the CDC website damages the credibility of federal health data at the worst possible moment, while kindergarten vaccination rates slide. In their view, silence from the top signals that politics is overriding science.

Seen systemically, U.S. disease control has always been a partnership: states investigate, the CDC aggregates and advises, and the public complies because it trusts the numbers. When that partnership frays, the damage is structural rather than personal — surveillance gaps and slower responses persist long after any single controversy fades.

The next steps matter most for children: whether the CDC publicly pushes on-time vaccination, whether states keep reporting deaths and cases into a shared system, and whether Congress or courts step in. If trust is not rebuilt, the cost shows up as preventable outbreaks in schools and communities for years to come.
